Overview

Somalia at a Glance

Somalia is a federal republic in which the Federal Government in Mogadishu shares authority with Federal Member States that issue their own business licences, while Somaliland administers its own institutions. Formal commercial law was rebuilt only recently: companies were long governed by the 1974 Civil Code supplemented by older Italian law, and a modern Companies Act was passed in December 2019 to create an Office of the Company Registrar and online registration. A Data Protection Act took effect in March 2023 and its Authority was launched in 2024. Records are fragmented, ownership data is often missing or outdated, and customary dispute resolution remains significant.

Organisations commission work touching Somalia because of its dense private networks in remittances, mobile money, telecommunications, livestock exports, ports, construction and imported goods, many linked to a large diaspora in East Africa, the Gulf, Europe and North America. Donors, humanitarian agencies, banks, correspondent banks, money transfer operators and investors need to know who they are dealing with. The principal exposures are diversion of funds, links to designated persons or armed groups, unclear beneficial ownership, conflicts between federal and state licensing, and reputational risk in procurement and logistics. Clients therefore ask for counterparty background research, ownership mapping and adverse-media and designation screening.

Legal Environment

How the law shapes investigative work involving Somalia

Legal system

Somalia has a mixed legal system combining codified civil law inherited from the Italian and post-independence period, including the Civil Code of 1974, Islamic law, and customary law. The Provisional Constitution of 2012 provides the current framework and recognises a right to privacy. Formal courts exist at federal and member-state level, but published World Bank analysis describes a long period of legal and regulatory vacuum in which businesses relied on traditional and customary dispute resolution with little formal enforcement. Practical forum and enforcement questions are therefore assessed case by case with Somali counsel, often alongside arbitration or courts abroad.

Data protection

Data Protection Act, 2023 (Law No. 005), in force from 23 March 2023, with implementing regulations · Regulator: Somalia Data Protection Authority (officially launched February 2024)

The Act gives individuals rights of access, correction, erasure, withdrawal of consent and objection, and protection from purely automated decisions. Processing requires a lawful basis such as consent or public interest. The Authority registers controllers and processors of major importance, can investigate and impose fines, and accredits data protection compliance organisations. Transfers outside Somalia are restricted unless the destination ensures adequate protection or safeguards such as contractual clauses or binding corporate rules apply; consent, contract and vital-interest exceptions are for occasional use only and must be notified to the Authority. Investigative work involving Somali personal data is scoped to a documented lawful basis, minimised and transferred on an assessed footing.

Private investigators

We have not identified a federal statute or authority that licenses private investigators or detective agencies in Somalia, and practice may differ in the Federal Member States and in Somaliland. The security environment is a decisive constraint: field enquiries can endanger sources, local staff and subjects, and must not involve payments or contact that could benefit armed or designated groups. Interception of communications and misuse of personal data raise exposure under the 2023 Act and general criminal law. TDSC therefore prioritises desk research, uses local professionals only where qualified, safe and lawful, and scopes any local step with Somali counsel.

Corporate & public records

The Companies Act passed in December 2019 established the Office of the Company Registrar within the Ministry of Commerce and Industry and the basis for online business registration, first rolled out in Mogadishu. Federal Member States continue to issue their own business licences and registration practice differs between states, while Somaliland maintains a separate system. Publicly searchable company data is limited, and World Bank analysis notes that company ownership information has often been missing or outdated. We have not identified a public federal beneficial ownership register. Land and court records are generally not available online and are obtained, where possible, through local counsel.

Anti-corruption & AML

Somalia enacted an Anti-Money Laundering and Countering the Financing of Terrorism framework in 2016, which applies customer due diligence obligations to banks and other reporting entities; research by the Hiraal Institute found that major businesses and banks had adopted due diligence systems ahead of formal requirements. Bribery and abuse of office are offences under the penal law. We have not verified the current status of a dedicated anti-corruption statute or commission for this page. Foreign clients typically rely on their own frameworks, such as the US Foreign Corrupt Practices Act or UK Bribery Act.

General information compiled 2026-11-04 from the sources listed below. It is not legal advice; TDSC works with qualified local counsel on questions of law.

Typical Matters

Where Investigative Work Involving Somalia Concentrates

01

Remittance and mobile money counterparties

Background and ownership research on hawala operators, money transfer agents and mobile money partners for banks, correspondent banks and payment firms, focusing on licensing, shareholder links, adverse media and any connection to designated persons or entities.

02

Humanitarian partner and contractor vetting

Integrity due diligence on implementing partners, transporters, landlords and suppliers for donors and agencies concerned about diversion and gatekeeping, drawing on registry information, diaspora corporate records abroad and lawful local enquiries where safe.

03

Port, logistics and import chains

Research on operators, shipping agents, importers and wholesalers connected to Mogadishu, Kismayo, Berbera and Bosaso, for insurers, traders and investors examining ownership, licensing across federal and state authorities, and enforcement or designation history.

04

Diaspora-linked corporate structures

Mapping of companies and individuals with interests in Somalia through registries in Kenya, the United Arab Emirates, the United Kingdom, the United States and elsewhere, where verifiable ownership and litigation records are often more complete than inside Somalia.

05

Telecoms and infrastructure investment

Pre-transaction due diligence on telecommunications, energy and construction businesses seeking investment or contracts, testing beneficial ownership, regulatory standing, related-party dealings and reputational risk before capital or equipment is committed.

Engagement Standard

How TDSC Scopes Matters Touching Somalia

TDSC scopes Somalia engagements from Nashville with a risk assessment that covers legal exposure, the physical safety of anyone involved and the possibility of indirectly benefiting designated groups. Most value comes from lawful sources outside the country: corporate and court records in diaspora jurisdictions, international sanctions and enforcement lists, trade and shipping data, and published reporting. Where Somali registry documents or local corroboration are needed, TDSC coordinates qualified local professionals and Somali counsel, specifies permitted methods in writing and rules out payments to intermediaries of unclear standing. Personal data is handled under the 2023 Act's lawful-basis and transfer rules. TDSC does not claim access to government systems, does not use pretexting and does not provide legal advice.

TDSC has no office in Somalia. Engagements are directed from Nashville, Tennessee; where work on the ground is needed, it is performed by appropriately licensed local professionals under a written scope. TDSC does not provide legal advice.

Questions

Somalia: Frequently Asked Questions

Is there a company registry in Somalia we can search?

The Companies Act of 2019 created an Office of the Company Registrar within the Ministry of Commerce and Industry and online registration, but public search capability is limited and ownership data has often been incomplete. Federal Member States license businesses separately and Somaliland runs its own system. TDSC combines what Somali sources provide with records in the jurisdictions where Somali-linked companies also register.

Does Somalia's data protection law apply to due diligence?

Yes, where Somali personal data is collected or processed. The Data Protection Act 2023 requires a lawful basis, grants data subject rights and restricts transfers abroad unless adequacy, approved safeguards or limited exceptions apply. The Somalia Data Protection Authority, launched in 2024, can investigate and fine. TDSC minimises personal data and documents the basis for each transfer to Nashville.

Can you send investigators into Somalia?

TDSC does not deploy its own staff to Somalia. Where a local step is lawful and genuinely necessary, it is undertaken by qualified local professionals after a security and legal assessment with Somali counsel. Many questions can be answered more safely and reliably from records held abroad, and some matters cannot be investigated in the field at all.

How do you address links to designated groups?

Screening against UN, US and other applicable designations is part of every Somalia-related engagement, together with research into ownership and associates. TDSC also designs its own work so that no payment, contact or service could benefit a designated person. Findings are presented with the evidence and its limits, so the client and its counsel can make the compliance decision.

Are Somaliland matters handled the same way?

Somaliland administers its own registration, licensing and courts, and records there are separate from federal systems in Mogadishu. TDSC treats it as a distinct records environment, identifies which authority holds the relevant information and scopes local steps with counsel familiar with Somaliland practice, while noting any cross-border or recognition issues the client should consider.
